flawed_step: The claim assumes that distinct arc capacities force a unique minimum cut. But different cuts can have the same capacity. For example, a vertex with no arcs can sit on either side of the cut without changing its capacity, and the definitions allow such vertices.
counterexample: V = {s, a, b, t}, with a single arc s->t of capacity 1; a and b have no arcs. The capacities are pairwise distinct because there is only one arc. The maximum flow is 1, which is positive. The s-t cuts are S = {s}, {s,a}, {s,b} and {s,a,b}. Each one has s->t as its only crossing arc, so each has capacity 1. That gives four distinct minimum cuts, not exactly one.
assessment_summary: The definitions allow isolated vertices. Moving an isolated vertex from one side of a cut to the other does not change the cut's capacity, so it creates a second minimum cut. The network with one arc s->t (capacity 1) and isolated vertices a and b satisfies every hypothesis and has 4 minimum cuts. The statement is false.
